opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the core issue is data. Language models were trained on essentially the entire internet: trillions of tokens of text that humans have been writing and posting for decades. When you add it up, it's on the order of what would take a person something like a hundred thousand years to read. We simply don't have anything comparable for robotics. There's no internet of robot motions, of what it actually feels like to grasp a slippery cup or fold a towel. So there's what I call a "hundred-thousand-year data gap" between where language models are and where robots are.

People say, "Well, we have all these YouTube videos of humans doing things." That's true, and it's useful, but video doesn't tell you the forces, the torques, the contact dynamics. You see a hand pick up a glass, but you don't see the friction, the pressure in the fingertips, the tiny corrections happening all the time. And those details are exactly what matter for a robot. Simulation helps too, but the gap between simulation and reality, the "sim-to-real" gap, is still very real, especially for contact and deformable objects.

Underneath all of this is something that's been understood for a long time: Moravec's paradox. The things we find hard, like chess, calculus, writing an essay, turn out to be relatively easy for computers. The things a two-year-old does effortlessly, like picking up a toy, stacking blocks, or walking across a cluttered room, turn out to be incredibly hard. We take them for granted because evolution spent hundreds of millions of years refining them. Language is a very recent invention by comparison, and it's in some sense a compressed, symbolic domain. The physical world isn't. It's continuous, noisy, and full of uncertainty in sensing, in control, and in the physics itself.

There's also the issue of stakes. If a language model makes a mistake, you get a bad sentence and you try again. If a robot makes a mistake, it drops your grandmother's china or it hurts someone. So the reliability bar is much higher, and getting from 90% to 99.9% success is where most of the hard work is.

I don't want to sound like a pessimist. I'm actually very excited about the progress. But I think we need to be realistic. The way through is going to be a combination of approaches: collecting real robot data, learning from video and simulation, and also, and I think this is underappreciated, good old-fashioned engineering. Physics, models, analytic methods. That's where a lot of the robustness comes from. The idea that we'll just scale up data and the problem will dissolve the way it seemed to for language is, I think, overly optimistic, at least on the timelines some people are suggesting.

r001.rationale: The response says language models were trained on enormous amounts of text, but does not attribute their generalisation to seeing a critical mass of similar patterns.

r002.rationale: It explains that robotics lacks comparable examples of robot motions and that videos omit forces and contact dynamics, leaving limited training data for predicting physical interactions.

r003.rationale: The response describes data scarcity and physical complexity, but does not say that high-dimensional robotics state spaces make enough examples difficult to obtain.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to appreciate is just how much data language models are trained on. We're talking about essentially the entire internet — trillions of words that humans have been writing and accumulating for decades. And that's what gave rise to these remarkable capabilities. People didn't necessarily predict that scale alone would get us there, but it did.

Now, in robotics, we don't have anything remotely like that. There's no internet of robot actions. Nobody's been recording what a robot's motors did and what its sensors saw while it folded laundry or picked something out of a bin, in a way that we could just scoop up and train on. The data we have is tiny by comparison — orders of magnitude smaller — and it's expensive to collect, because you actually have to run a physical robot in the real world, and that takes time, it breaks things, you need people supervising.

And then there's a second problem, which is that the physical world is just much less forgiving than text. If a language model makes a small error in word choice, it's usually fine, the meaning comes through. But if a robot's gripper is off by a centimetre, it misses the object, or knocks over the glass. Perception is noisy, friction is unpredictable, objects deform. I like to say that physics is messy in ways that don't show up in a text corpus. Even things like the exact position of a cable or how a towel is going to crumple — these are things we still can't reliably simulate.

So you have this double challenge: far less data, and a domain where small inaccuracies compound into failures. That's why I'm a bit cautious when people say we're one or two years from a general-purpose robot. I'm optimistic about the direction — the progress on things like learning from demonstration and using foundation models for high-level reasoning is real — but closing that gap is, I think, a much longer road than the language model trajectory would suggest.

r001.rationale: It credits language models’ capabilities to training scale, but does not say they generalise by encountering a critical mass of similar patterns.

r002.rationale: It describes scarce robotics data and physical-world errors, but does not explain that unfamiliar domains are hard to predict because training samples provide little basis for them.

r003.rationale: It says robotics data is much smaller and costly to collect, but does not identify high-dimensional robotics state spaces as the reason enough examples are daunting.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the big differences is the data. Language models can learn from this enormous body of text that people have already produced. In robotics, we don’t have anything comparable that captures actions and their consequences: what the robot sensed, how it moved, what forces it applied, and what happened next.

And the physical world is very unforgiving. If I’m picking up a glass, a small change in its position, or its weight, or the friction between the glass and the gripper can make the difference between success and failure. Seeing a lot of pictures of glasses doesn’t necessarily tell you how to handle those differences.

There’s also a practical problem with collecting experience. You can process text very quickly, but a robot has to move through the world. Things take time, things wear out, and someone may have to reset the experiment when it fails.

So I’m excited about what we can transfer from language models. But going from recognising or describing a situation to reliably acting in it—that’s a substantial additional challenge.

r002.rationale: It describes the lack of robotics experience data and the difficulty of acting reliably, but does not explain that training samples provide little basis for predictions in an unfamiliar domain.

r003.rationale: The response discusses physical variability and the time and effort required to collect robot experience, but does not mention the high dimensionality of robotics state spaces.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, a robot has to connect what it understands to what actually happens in the physical world. And that world is extraordinarily varied. Take picking up a glass: you have to deal with its geometry, its weight, whether it’s slippery, whether it’s full, and what’s around it. Small differences can change what you need to do, and some of those properties aren’t visible until you make contact.

Language models benefit from enormous amounts of text that people have already produced. We don’t have an equivalent amount of robot experience. Collecting that experience is slow: you need hardware, you need to reset things, and things break. Simulation helps, but modelling contact and friction accurately is difficult, so something that works in simulation may fail on the real robot.

And then there’s the feedback loop. A robot’s actions change the situation it’s trying to understand. It has to sense, act, and correct itself continually. So language models are very exciting for robotics, but being able to describe how to do something is still quite different from being able to do it reliably.

r001.rationale: The response says language models benefit from enormous amounts of text, but does not connect their generalisation to seeing a critical mass of similar patterns in training examples.

r002.rationale: It describes the difficulty of transferring simulation results to real robots, but does not explain that unfamiliar domains are hard to predict because training samples provide little basis for those predictions.

r003.rationale: The response describes varied physical properties and scarce robot experience, but does not attribute the data challenge to the high dimensionality of robotics state spaces.
